title: From 'polycrisis' to 'polytunity' - the future of geopolitics with Prof Yuen Yuen Ang
gist: Johns Hopkins political economist Yuen Yuen Ang, interviewed at the WEF Annual Meeting of the New Champions in Dalian, argues the 'polycrisis' is really a crisis of Western decline and a 'polytunity' for the global majority, and that China's central problem is an economic paradox: dazzling 0-to-1 tech (AI, quantum, EVs, aeronautics) that creates almost no mass employment, sitting on top of a dead old growth model, which is why domestic consumption stays weak and Chinese output must be exported as a 'China shock'. Her fix is 'humble innovation' - traditional industries, e-commerce, modular manufacturing in Shenzhen - plus a rewiring of local-official incentives that currently reward flying taxis and dancing robots.

insights.claim: The term 'polycrisis' was popularised by Adam Tooze at the World Economic Forum in 2023 to name an entanglement of global threats, and Yuen Yuen Ang argues it should be flipped to 'polytunity' because a fear-driven frame is paralysing rather than actionable.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: The elite narrative frame is rotating from risk-avoidance to opportunity-seeking; expect Davos-adjacent policy language and allocation to follow that rotation.
insights.quote: the idea of a polycrisis is frankly, fear-driven, paralysing
insights.locator: the term polycrisis was actually popularised at this very forum

insights.claim: Periods of systemic breakdown are the only realistic windows for deep structural transformation, because in normal times incumbents keep running business as usual no matter how broken the system is.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Treat the current breakdown as a forcing function: reform windows in trade, industrial policy and institutions open now and close when stability returns.
insights.quote: in normal times, we don't like to make big changes. It's hard. It's risky. So we'll continue with business as usual, no matter how broken things are.
insights.locator: in normal times, we don't like to make big changes

insights.claim: Ang contends the polycrisis is primarily a crisis of Western decline, not a global one, because power has already shifted to Africa, Asia and Latin America as well as China, and the 'global majority' now expects to set agendas rather than receive them.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Risk-premium narratives built out of Washington and Brussels systematically overstate global fragility and understate emerging-market agency and demand.
insights.quote: I think the term polycrisis is more of a polycrisis of Western decline. Not a critique of the West, just a statement of observation.
insights.locator: so in many ways, I think the term polycrisis

insights.claim: Complaining about the polycrisis does not resonate outside the West, because for most of the world today's mix of risk and opportunity is better than anything available in the last century.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Sentiment gaps between developed-market and emerging-market decision-makers are structural, not cyclical - a reason EM capex intentions can stay firm while DM confidence sags.
insights.quote: if you sit here and moan about the polycrisis, it doesn't resonate with the rest of the world
insights.locator: And so that's why if you sit here and moan

themes.theme: How globalisation trapped China in cheap goods

insights.claim: The globalisation order that let China prosper through export-led manufacturing also trapped it: because consumer-goods manufacturing was so profitable, state pressure to climb the value chain, form joint ventures and do fundamental R&D repeatedly failed.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Industrial upgrading in China was demand-constrained by profitability, not capability - which is why external shock, not subsidy, was the effective catalyst.
insights.quote: Because why would you work, why would you really do the hard thing when you make so much profit from doing consumer manufacturing?
insights.locator: despite state efforts to compel, pressure Chinese companies

insights.claim: The head-on US-China competition that began around 2016 functioned as China's 'polytunity' - the threat that finally justified abandoning shoes, toys and toasters for advanced materials, aeroplanes and quantum computers under the 14th and 15th Five-Year Plans.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: US pressure accelerated rather than blunted Chinese upgrading; further decoupling should be modelled as an accelerant of Chinese upstream capability, not a brake.
insights.quote: given that the state of the world is in disorder, anyway, let's take advantage of that and do the hard thing
insights.locator: So in a sense when China and the U.S. had this head-on competition

themes.theme: China's economic paradox and the consumption bottleneck

insights.claim: Ang's 'China economic paradox' is that real, impressive high-tech advances coexist with a broad economic slowdown - the country's core problem is neither the growth slowdown alone nor geopolitical tension alone.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Do not read Chinese tech breakthroughs as a proxy for Chinese macro strength - the two series can diverge for years.
insights.quote: the high-tech advances are real and they are impressive, but they are coexisting with a broad economic slowdown
insights.locator: It's in particular what I call China's economic paradox

insights.claim: Production and consumption are a single system in China: without domestic consumption power, the EVs and advanced materials China builds must be pushed out to Southeast Asia, South Africa and other markets, which is what the world experiences as the 'China shock'.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Weak Chinese retail demand is a direct leading indicator of export volume, global goods deflation and trade-friction risk in EM markets.
insights.quote: if you don't have a domestic consumption power, then they have to go out
insights.locator: And so China is making these EVs, advanced materials

insights.claim: Boosting Chinese domestic consumption has stopped being a domestic policy question and become an international one, because it is the only mechanism that keeps Chinese production sustainable without triggering foreign backlash.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Chinese consumption stimulus is the key variable for global trade-war de-escalation - watch it as a geopolitical, not just cyclical, indicator.
insights.quote: boosting Chinese domestic consumption is no longer a domestic issue. It actually is an international issue
insights.locator: Then the key to that is consumption

insights.claim: China's second-highest-ranking official used the Dalian opening plenary to push back on the Western 'China shock 2.0' narrative and recast it as 'China opportunity 2.0', but Ang insists the shock is real and must be acknowledged because other countries legitimately ask what is left for them to make.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Beijing's official framing understates the trade-conflict risk embedded in its own export surge; expect more tariff and local-content responses abroad.
insights.quote: So that is the shock. And the shock is real. It has to be acknowledged.
insights.locator: But China is just so good at manufacturing

insights.claim: Chinese retail sales fell 0.6% last month, the first decline in more than three years, even as eight central government departments announced an acceleration of 'AI plus consumption' development - a gap between policy activity and measured results.
insights.speaker: Olivia Siong
insights.so_what: Hard evidence that Chinese consumption stimulus is not yet transmitting - a live short-term risk for consumer-exposed China names and a support for the export-push thesis.
insights.quote: retail sales fell by 0.6% and that was for the first time in more than three years
insights.locator: but the statistic we saw last year, last month rather

insights.claim: Consumption policy has an intrinsically slower and less controllable transmission mechanism than investment: a government can pump billions and see a GDP effect, but cannot press a button and get consumption three months later.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Explains Beijing's revealed preference for investment stimulus and warns against expecting fast consumption prints after each announced package.
insights.quote: It's almost like dealing with AI. You know, you thought you put in all the right inputs, why am I not getting the right outputs, right?
insights.locator: Because consumption is slow

insights.claim: The root cause of persistently weak Chinese consumption is employment structure: the new growth model of AI, quantum, EVs and aeronautics is not mass-employment-producing and may cut jobs in the short term, while the weakened old growth model no longer employs hundreds of millions plus each year's college-graduate cohort.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: The consumption weakness is structural and multi-year, not a confidence blip - underwrite Chinese consumer demand recovery slowly.
insights.quote: when I go to one of these impressive automated factories in China, I'm like, wow, this is so sleek. There is nobody in this factory. They're all robots. So where are the jobs?
insights.locator: The new growth models impressive advances

insights.claim: Targeted subsidies such as EV trade-in grants give only temporary demand boosts and cannot fix Chinese consumption, because the true driver is job security - people spend when they have a good job and feel safe in it.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Fade the consumption impact of each new Chinese subsidy programme; track labour-market and graduate-employment data instead.
insights.quote: the fundamental fix of consumption is employment. I have a good job, I feel safe in my job. I feel confident, I spend.
insights.locator: The solution will not be a quick fix

insights.claim: Ang argues China is over-allocating to cutting-edge, marketable technologies and under-allocating to traditional industries and applicational innovation such as e-commerce, which are the sectors that actually generate mass employment and are open to people from all walks of life.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: A policy pivot toward 'boring' sectors would be the real signal that Beijing is serious about consumption - and a rerating catalyst for old-economy Chinese names.
insights.quote: too much emphasis is being placed on the cutting-edge technologies right now. They are impressive, they're marketable, and too little emphasis is being placed on everything else
insights.locator: So I think that one of the key solutions

insights.claim: China's most underrated industrial asset is modular manufacturing: a comprehensive, nimble supply chain lets an entrepreneur from Switzerland or Singapore go to Shenzhen, prototype a product and run a small batch quickly and cheaply, replacing the old model of gigantic single-product MNC factories.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Small-batch prototyping capacity is a durable Chinese moat that tariffs do not touch and that reshoring plans rarely replicate - relevant for hardware startup supply chains.
insights.quote: an entrepreneur from any part of the world, Switzerland, Singapore, can go to Shenzhen and say, I want to prototype a new product, and can I make a small batch of it?
insights.locator: What is modular manufacturing?

insights.claim: Ang's core distinction is between 'humble innovation' - low barriers to entry, broad participation, easily integrated into daily life - and 'glamorous innovation', which matters only in particular contexts; she says the real solution to Chinese consumption lies in the non-glamorous parts of the economy.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: A reusable screen for industrial policy anywhere: ask how many people can participate in the innovation, not how advanced it is.
insights.quote: the real solution to consumption in China has to come from humble innovation, humble. Humble in the sense that everyone can participate, the barriers of entry are low
insights.locator: In the end, the real solution to consumption in China

insights.claim: Ang implies the bias toward glamorous technology is geopolitical rather than economic - modular manufacturing is ignored precisely because it wins no geopolitical chips, while headline AI, quantum and dancing robots do.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Expect continued state capital misallocation toward showcase tech as long as technology doubles as diplomatic currency.
insights.quote: it's not fancy, it not glamorous, it doesn't win China geopolitical chips, right. We much prefer the headline AI, quantum, dancing robots.
insights.locator: But you see, we don't talk about that

insights.claim: The same misallocation risk applies in the West, where enormous sums are being poured into AI without clear knowledge of the applications while governments and companies neglect humbler innovation - a framing Ang endorses without qualification.
insights.speaker: Robin Pomeroy
insights.so_what: A mainstream WEF-platform voicing of AI capex scepticism - watch for this framing migrating into policy and allocator language.
insights.quote: There's so much money being poured into AI without potentially knowing exactly what the applications for some of these things are.
insights.locator: I wonder if that's the case in the West as well

insights.claim: The K-shaped economy language is now used in both Washington and Beijing: in the US tech companies grow ever more powerful while ordinary Americans are fed up with data centres built around them consuming their water, and Ang was surprised to hear Chinese officials adopt the same K-shaped framing at Summer Davos.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Local water and siting backlash against data centres is now cited at Davos as a mainstream political constraint - a rising permitting risk for AI infrastructure buildouts.
insights.quote: the tech companies are becoming ever more powerful, while ordinary Americans are fed up with data centres being built around them and using up their water
insights.locator: a lot of people talk about the K-shaped economy in the U.S.

insights.claim: A recurring Ang thesis is that despite appearing to be rivals, China and America share far more structurally - including inequality dynamics and tech-sector concentration - than most observers recognise.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Convergent domestic political pressures in both powers make symmetric policy responses (tech backlash, employment-first industrial policy) more likely than divergent ones.
insights.quote: China and America have a lot more in common than most people realise
insights.locator: So despite seeming to be rivals

themes.theme: Five-Year Plan as steering wheel and signalling tool

insights.claim: The 14th Five-Year Plan had a singular goal of cutting-edge technology under the 'new productive forces' banner, while the 15th adds consumption on top of it - and Ang calls that addition necessary rather than trivial, a pairing repeated at the central economic work conference.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Read the consumption language in the 15th FYP as a structural commitment rather than boilerplate - it is the precondition for China's export model surviving.
insights.quote: it's not a trivial add-on. It's a necessary add-on
insights.locator: If you look the 15 five- year plan, consumption has been added

insights.claim: Ang's driving analogy: five-year plans through the 13th were autopilot within a settled paradigm of global integration, FDI, exports, real estate and construction, whereas from the 14th onward China has both hands on a very heavy steering wheel trying to turn a gigantic tanker.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Sets expectations for turn radius: a tanker turn means multi-plan timelines, so bet on persistence of the policy direction rather than speed of results.
insights.quote: it's a very heavy steering wheel because we are not talking about, we're not talking about a light sedan, not even an SUV, it's gigantic tanker and China is trying to make a right turn
insights.locator: The analogy that I used was that five-year plans

insights.claim: The central party leadership is now personally supervising the drafting of the five-year plan, which has been elevated within China's political system into a signalling tool - explaining why the plan suddenly commands global attention.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Treat FYP text as the highest-fidelity available signal of Chinese capital allocation - its sectoral emphasis is a tradable roadmap.
insights.quote: the central party leadership is now personally supervising, drafting the five-year Plan. It has, in China's political system, been elevated as a signalling tool.
insights.locator: Now why is it that from the 14 and 15 Five-Year Plan onward

insights.claim: China's 'right turn' has two levels: first a shift from quantity to quality of GDP - abandoning the old 7-12% growth built on low-end manufacturing, real-estate overcapacity and pollution - and second a structural change in the type of innovation the country pursues.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Beijing has explicitly deprioritised headline growth, so weak GDP prints should not be read as policy failure or as a trigger for a real-estate bailout.
insights.quote: in the past China had, and it was normal for China to have 7, even 12% GDP growth, but a lot of it just came from low-hanging fruits
insights.locator: There are two levels. The first transformation

insights.claim: Ang's 0-to-1 / 1-to-10 / 10-to-100 framework: China has been good at applying others' inventions (1 to 10) and singularly good at scaling them cheaply thanks to its massive market (10 to 100, as in green energy), and since the 14th Five-Year Plan has added the ambition of upstream 0-to-1 invention - a term now trending on WeChat.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: A clean lens for judging Chinese tech claims: scaling wins are proven, upstream invention is the unproven leg where capital and policy risk concentrate.
insights.quote: we want to have a structural transformation in the kinds of innovation we are good at
insights.locator: The level two is in addition to that

insights.claim: The trigger for China's upstream push was discovering it could manufacture everything except what sits upstream - when the US cut off chip supply, China found itself helpless, which is what turned '0 to 1' into a national ambition.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Export controls are the direct cause of China's upstream capital cycle; further controls should be expected to deepen, not deter, domestic substitution spending.
insights.quote: when the U S cuts off supply to chips, China finds that it was helpless. And so it realised that it has to move upstream.
insights.locator: China realised that we are good at manufacturing everything except everything that's upstream

insights.claim: Ang's prescription for the 16th Five-Year Plan is to stop pouring every cent into 0-to-1 innovation and instead balance across all innovation types, because upstream invention does not produce jobs.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: If the 16th FYP tilts back toward employment-generating sectors, it validates a rotation from Chinese frontier-tech to consumer and traditional-industry exposure.
insights.quote: you can only solve the consumption problem by making sure that you are doing all kinds of innovation and not just pouring every cent you have into zero to one innovation, because that doesn't produce jobs
insights.locator: 16th five year plan. What's the direction?

insights.claim: China's misallocation is enforced by bureaucratic career incentives: because implementation is local and the plan makes priorities explicit, an official gains nothing from reviving real estate or traditional industry and everything from showcasing a flying taxi or dancing robots.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Until cadre evaluation metrics change, expect continued overcapacity in showcase sectors regardless of central rhetoric about consumption.
insights.quote: You want to stand out by saying, I have a flying taxi. Or I have dancing robots, right.
insights.locator: Right now, try to imagine being a Chinese official

themes.theme: Manufacturing migration and the developing-country squeeze

insights.claim: Contrary to the premise that automation has stalled the relocation of manufacturing out of China, Ang says the migration is actively happening, with many Chinese companies moving overseas and specialist intermediaries connecting them to Southeast Asia as diversification and risk management.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: China+1 capacity buildout is being financed by Chinese firms themselves - watch ASEAN industrial-park and supplier names as the beneficiaries.
insights.quote: in fact that migration is happening. There are many Chinese companies moving overseas.
insights.locator: How do you see China's role, either good or bad, in developing countries

insights.claim: Developing economies will not settle for inheriting low-end consumer manufacturing: Malaysia has semiconductor ambitions, other economies want to build their own cars, and even Vietnam wants to make its own EVs - which puts them on a collision course with cheap high-quality Chinese exports.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Expect rising local-content rules, tariffs and JV requirements across ASEAN and Africa aimed at Chinese autos and electronics.
insights.quote: you have countries like Malaysia has aspirations in doing some semiconductor manufacturing, right? Other economies also want to make their own cars. Even Vietnam wants to make its own EVs.
insights.locator: perhaps certain countries might be content taking over the low-end

insights.claim: Ang's ideal resolution to the China-shock problem for developing countries is reciprocal demand - Chinese consumers buying from them - rather than joint ventures or Chinese investment alone.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Chinese import growth from emerging markets, not Chinese FDI outflows, is the metric that would signal a genuinely rebalanced trade relationship.
insights.quote: I think that the ideal answer would be that Chinese consumers also buy from them
insights.locator: Maybe it's the joint ventures or Chinese investment

insights.claim: The hope that low-quality mass manufacturing simply migrates from China to poorer countries is undercut by automation and by China's own need to keep those jobs at home given high domestic unemployment.
insights.speaker: Robin Pomeroy
insights.so_what: The classic flying-geese development path may not repeat, which caps the industrialisation upside priced into frontier-market growth stories.
insights.quote: There's not much indication that will happen, particularly as it's automated, particularly because you've got a lot of unemployment here.
insights.locator: it might be hoped that some of that lower quality mass-produced manufacturing

insights.claim: The US-China relationship has stabilised and feels much more amiable following President Trump's visit to Beijing, with more meetings expected in the year ahead, though Ang stresses the underlying competition continues regardless.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Near-term de-escalation is real and tradable, but should not be extrapolated into structural détente on tech or trade controls.
insights.quote: It's a very encouraging sign. I think the last visit that at least the relationship feels much more amiable. But the competition will go on and on, right?
insights.locator: the relationship has stabilised following President Trump's visit to Beijing

insights.claim: Washington's central analytical trap is a Cold War mindset held by decision-makers who personally lived through it, producing an expectation of zero-sum competition ending in one side's collapse and a clear victory party.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: US policy will keep being calibrated to a collapse scenario that will not arrive, raising the odds of persistent, unresolved friction rather than clean resolution.
insights.quote: they also have this expectation that like in the Cold War, the end game is that one side will fall. And then you have complete victory, you have a big party, and then yay, right?
insights.locator: I think that the trap that often happens

insights.claim: Ang predicts the US-China contest will have no endgame and no clear victor for a long time to come, making an indefinite stalemate the base case rather than either side's collapse.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Price permanent bifurcation - dual supply chains, standing export controls, no resolution - rather than either escalation to conflict or reconciliation.
insights.quote: it's possible that there will be no end game, no clear victor for a long time to come
insights.locator: The two big powers are in a competition

insights.claim: Third countries are no longer passive: Singapore in particular, and others generally, are explicitly refusing to pick sides and will do business with both great powers as their interests dictate - a reality the US still has to adapt to.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Alignment-forcing US policies will underperform; hedging middle powers are structural beneficiaries of dual-track trade and investment flows.
insights.quote: we're not going to pick sides. We're going to do business with both great powers, however it fits our interests
insights.locator: It's also a new world where the rest of the world is no longer just passive

insights.claim: Ang deliberately named her Johns Hopkins forum the 'Multi-Polar World and US-China Forum', putting multipolarity first because US-China debate is over-centred on Washington and Beijing while everyone else now has more agency than at any point in the 20th century.
insights.speaker: Yuen Yuen Ang
insights.so_what: Analytical frameworks that model the world as a two-player game will systematically miss where the marginal decisions - and marginal demand - are actually made.
insights.quote: Everyone else wants to have a voice and they have more agency today than they ever did in the 20th century.
insights.locator: At Johns Hopkins, I run a forum called the Multi-Polar World
